# Viapunt guide (English)

The pages of the Viapunt naturalisation guide for the canton of Zurich, as published. Each page also exists in German and, as drafts, in six more languages.

## Page: Becoming Swiss: How Naturalisation Works

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/overview/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/ueberblick/  
Last checked: 2026-10-30

## Ordinary naturalisation

If you want to become a Swiss citizen and you are not married to a Swiss person, you will usually use **ordinary naturalisation**. It runs through three levels: commune, canton and Confederation. It often takes several years.

## Federal requirements

The State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) names these points for ordinary naturalisation:

- **Settlement permit C.** You need a valid C permit.
- **Ten years of residence in Switzerland.** Three of them must fall in the last five years before you apply. Years with a B or C permit count in full, years with an F permit count by half. Years with an N or L permit do not count.
- **Years between your 8th and 18th birthdays count double.** But you must still have lived in Switzerland for at least six actual years. Our [calculator]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/calculator/) can give you a rough count.
- **Language.** At least level B1 spoken and at least level A2 written in a national language. Cantons may ask for more. See [Language certificates]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/language-certificates/).
- **Respect for public safety and order** and for the values of the Federal Constitution.
- **Taking part in economic life or in education.**
- **No social assistance in the three years before you apply**, unless you have repaid it in full.
- **Familiarity with Swiss living conditions.** Many cantons check this with a test. In the canton of Zurich it is the [knowledge test]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/knowledge-test/).
- You support the integration of your family members and do not endanger Switzerland's security.

Cantons can add conditions, for example a minimum period of residence in the canton and commune. The SEM mentions two to five years.

## Commune, canton, Confederation

Swiss citizenship has three levels. Whoever becomes Swiss receives citizenship of a commune and of a canton at the same time.

The order of steps in short:

1. You file your application with your commune or canton of residence. The canton decides which office is responsible.
2. The canton, and usually the commune, check whether you meet the requirements. This includes language and basic knowledge.
3. The canton passes the application to the SEM. The SEM grants the federal naturalisation permit.
4. The canton takes its final decision within one year of that permit.
5. You become a citizen once the cantonal decision is legally binding.

The detailed procedure for Zurich is on the page [Zurich, step by step]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/zurich-step-by-step/).

## How long does it take?

The SEM gives no overall time. The canton of Zurich says on its page that the procedure takes about two years. A 2025 study by the canton shows that communes are receiving more applications and processing takes longer on average. Expect waiting times and ask your commune for the current duration.

## Simplified naturalisation

Some groups can use a simpler procedure that runs directly through the Confederation.

- **Spouses of Swiss citizens** can be naturalised in a simplified way under certain conditions. Those living in Switzerland need five years of residence in total and three years of marriage.
- **The third generation of foreign nationals** can apply if they were born in Switzerland, went to school here for at least five years, and apply before their 25th birthday. Further conditions concern parents and grandparents.

The full conditions and fees are on the SEM pages (in German): [spouses](https://www.sem.admin.ch/sem/de/home/integration-einbuergerung/schweizer-werden/verheiratet.html) and [third generation](https://www.sem.admin.ch/sem/de/home/integration-einbuergerung/schweizer-werden/3-generation.html).

## Who to ask

- The **citizenship office of your commune**. It knows the local rules and dates.
- In the canton of Zurich, the **Gemeindeamt, naturalisation section** (telephone +41 43 259 83 81).
- For questions about your own case: an advice service or a lawyer.

## Next step

In the canton of Zurich a knowledge test is part of the procedure. Try our free practice questions and see how well prepared you already are.

## Page: Naturalisation in the Canton of Zurich, Step by Step

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/zurich-step-by-step/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/zuerich-schritt-fuer-schritt/  
Last checked: 2026-10-30

## Before you start

In the canton of Zurich you file the application online with the canton's **Gemeindeamt** (office for communes), which runs the procedure. Your **commune of residence** then checks your integration and grants communal citizenship. The canton offers a free, non-binding self-check on its website that shows whether you are likely to meet the requirements.

## Residence in commune and canton

On top of the federal rules (C permit, ten years in Switzerland, three of them in the last five years), Zurich has these periods:

- **Commune:** immediately before you apply you must have lived in the **same commune for at least two years**.
- **Canton:** if you are under 25, you only need two years in the canton of Zurich. The canton's self-check lists two years in the canton as an example of a condition. The canton's pages do not say clearly whether a longer period applies from age 25; the Gemeindeamt can tell you.

Moving to another Zurich commune during the procedure may be possible. Tell your commune at once.

## The steps

The canton describes five steps:

1. **Preliminary check** by the Gemeindeamt (canton).
2. **Check by your commune of residence.** If it succeeds, you receive communal citizenship.
3. **Second check** by the Gemeindeamt. If it succeeds, you receive cantonal citizenship.
4. **Check by the SEM** (Confederation). It grants the naturalisation permit.
5. **Final check** by the Gemeindeamt, which grants Swiss citizenship.

## Documents

Everyone in the application attaches two documents: a civil status document (at most 6 months old) and proof of current work or education (at most 3 months old). Proof of German and basic knowledge comes on top if you already have it. The authorities fetch the debt collection register, criminal record and welfare information themselves, and communes may not add requirements of their own. The full list, where to get each document, costs and how old it may be: [Documents]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/documents/).

## Language and basic knowledge

Two proofs are part of the procedure:

- **German:** B1 spoken, A2 written. You can show this with a recognised certificate or with the Cantonal German Test. See [Language certificates]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/language-certificates/).
- **Knowledge test:** knowledge of Switzerland, the canton of Zurich and the commune. See [Knowledge test]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/knowledge-test/).

You can take both tests before or after you file the application. Your commune tells you what applies there.

## Interview with the commune

Communes check how well you are integrated, for example language, basic knowledge and contact with Swiss people. Many communes hold a personal interview or hearing for this. According to the canton's 2025 study, 51 per cent of communes always held an interview, down from 71 per cent in 2022. The canton's page on ordinary naturalisation does not mention an interview. Ask your commune whether there is one and what form it takes.

## How long does it take?

The canton says the procedure takes **about two years**. The 2025 study shows that processing in the communes takes longer on average than before: about a quarter of communes reported an average of more than six months for their part, against about a tenth in 2022. After the federal permit, the canton has one year to take its decision.

## Costs

The Confederation and the canton charge fixed fees. Each commune sets its own fee, so it differs from place to place. All figures are on the page [Fees]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/fees/).

## Next step

For many people the knowledge test is the biggest thing to study. The free questions show you how you are doing.

## Page: Documents for Naturalisation in Zurich

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/documents/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/unterlagen/  
Last checked: 2026-10-30

## What you attach

Since 1 July 2023 the canton of Zurich has had one set of rules for every commune. You file the application online with the canton's **Gemeindeamt** (office for communes), not with your commune. For every person in the application you attach **two documents** (KBüV § 7):

1. a document from the civil status office showing your civil status, and
2. proof that you work, are in education, or otherwise support yourself.

You add proof of German and proof of basic knowledge **if you already have them**, plus a few documents that apply only in some situations (see the tables below).

You do **not** collect a debt collection extract, a criminal record extract, a tax certificate or a welfare confirmation. The authorities get these themselves. The canton also says that communes may not set conditions of their own. They only organise their part of the procedure.

Apply online at [zh.ch/e-einbuergerung](https://www.zh.ch/e-einbuergerung). Questions: your commune or the Gemeindeamt (043 259 83 81, einbuergerungen.gaz@ji.zh.ch).

## How old documents may be

The canton's checklist sets two limits on the day you **submit**:

- **Civil status document:** at most **6 months** old.
- **All other documents:** at most **3 months** old.

So order them last, shortly before you submit. The checklist does not say whether the 3-month limit also applies to certificates you earned earlier, such as school reports or language certificates. Ask your commune.

## Start here: are you in the Swiss civil status register?

Without the civil status document your application is not processed. If you were born or married abroad, you may **not yet be registered** in the Swiss register. If so, register first, because this is often the slowest step:

- **City of Zurich:** fill in the city's online form "Registration in the civil status register". The office then emails you a list of the documents it needs. The city says registration can take **several weeks to several months**.
- **Other communes:** ask the civil status office for your area. Uster, for example, asks for a copy of your residence permit and your passport or ID card.
- **Documents from abroad** (birth or marriage certificate) usually have to be **legalised or carry an apostille** in the country that issued them, and may need a translation. Zurich authorities do not translate. Events abroad can also be reported through the Swiss embassy or consulate.

Once you are registered, ordering the document itself is quick. In the city of Zurich a proof of civil status (Personenstandsausweis) costs **CHF 30 plus CHF 1.20 postage**.

## Documents you provide

| Document | Who needs it | Where to get it | Cost | Maximum age when you submit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Civil status document** (for example proof of civil status or family record) | Everyone in the application | Civil status office (Zivilstandsamt). City of Zurich: order online. | City of Zurich: CHF 30 plus postage. Other offices: ask. | 6 months |
| **Proof of current activity** (see next table) | Everyone aged 12 or over | Your employer, school, unemployment fund, pension fund and so on. The city of Zurich has an employer form to download. | Usually free | 3 months |
| **Proof of German** (B1 spoken, A2 written), if you already have it | Everyone aged 12 or over, unless German is your mother tongue | School reports (5 years of compulsory school in German), a diploma taught in German, a current school confirmation, or a recognised certificate (KDE, telc, ÖSD, Goethe, fide). See [Language certificates]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/language-certificates/). | Test fees vary; the KDE costs CHF 200 to 280 in the communes below | See "How long are certificates valid?" |
| **Proof of basic knowledge**, if you already have it | Everyone aged 12 or over | School reports (5 years of compulsory school in Switzerland, 3 of them at lower-secondary level), a Swiss upper-secondary qualification, a current school confirmation, or the knowledge test certificate. See [Knowledge test]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/knowledge-test/). | Test CHF 100 to 250, depending on the commune | See below |
| Proof of sole custody, or consent of both parents | Only if minor children are included | Divorce judgment, custody arrangement or decision of the child protection authority (KESB). With joint custody both parents sign the signature sheet in the online form. | Depends on the court or office | 3 months |
| Declaration on registered partnership and proof of your partner's citizenship | Only if you want the shorter residence periods for registered partners | Both partners sign in the online form. Proof of citizenship from the civil status office of your partner's place of origin. | Ask the office | 3 months |
| Proof of personal circumstances (for example a medical certificate) | Only if illness, disability or similar reasons stop you from meeting a requirement such as the German test | Your doctor or another specialist. It must say exactly what you cannot do and why. | You pay for it (KBüV § 16) | Not stated; ask your commune |

If you do not yet have proof of German or basic knowledge, your commune tells you when and where to take the test. Some communes want both before you file, others after (see "What differs between communes").

## Proof of current activity

| Your situation | What to provide |
| --- | --- |
| Employed | Current confirmation from your employer |
| Self-employed | Copy of pages 1 to 4 of your latest tax return |
| Unemployed and receiving benefits | Unemployment benefit statements for the last 3 months |
| Receiving payments from others | Statement from AHV/IV, SUVA, health insurance, pension fund, maintenance payments, grants and so on |
| Homemaker | Proof of the family's income, for example a bank statement or pages 1 to 4 of the latest tax return |
| Not working and no benefits | Proof of assets, for example a bank statement |
| In training or further education | Current confirmation from the school or course |
| At school | Current school confirmation or a copy of the school report |

## What the authorities get themselves

| Check | Who gets it | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Debt collection register (unpaid debts, including tax debts, from 5 years before you apply) | Gemeindeamt | KBüV § 4 (3) |
| Criminal record (federal register VOSTRA) | Gemeindeamt | Canton's handbook |
| Social welfare received in the last 3 years | Your commune | KBüV § 15 |

You do not need to order a debt collection extract (CHF 17), a criminal record extract or a residence certificate for ordinary naturalisation. If someone asks you for one, ask which rule requires it. Lists that still mention such papers, for example in Winterthur's fee overview, refer to **facilitated** naturalisation (for example through marriage), which has different rules.

## What differs between communes

Communes cannot add requirements, but they do differ in when you take the tests, whether there is an interview, and the fee. A sample from commune websites and guides, checked in October 2026:

| Commune | Tests | Interview | Communal fee, adult 25+ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| City of Zurich | German test (KDE, CHF 250) after you file, if you have no certificate | Only if questions remain | Not stated on the city's page |
| Winterthur | Not stated. KDE CHF 250, knowledge test CHF 150. | Yes, by the city's naturalisation department (not confirmed on its page) | CHF 1,200 (20 to 24: CHF 600; under 20: free) |
| Uster | Both proofs **before** you file | Not mentioned | CHF 1,380 single, CHF 1,910 couple or family; free up to age 25 |
| Dübendorf | Not stated. Knowledge test CHF 175, KDE CHF 280. | Not on its page | CHF 1,000 (20 to 24: CHF 500; under 20: free) |
| Bülach | Both tests **before** you file | Normally none | CHF 1,000, couple CHF 1,500. Tests CHF 250 each. |
| Wädenswil | Knowledge test information is sent **after** you file | Not stated | Not stated |
| Otelfingen (small commune) | Both tests **before** you file | Normally none | CHF 500. KDE CHF 200, knowledge test CHF 100. |

If your commune holds an interview, the law gives you rights: you choose Standard German or Swiss German, you may bring an adult companion, and the commune keeps minutes or a recording. Children under 12 are not interviewed (KBüV §§ 13 and 14). Cantonal and federal fees are on the page [Fees]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/fees/).

## How long are certificates valid?

- **Language certificates:** neither the canton nor the SEM sets a fixed expiry. A certificate counts if it was on the SEM list of recognised certificates on the day you submit. The authority may ask for a new assessment, especially if the certificate was issued a long time ago. If you send an original, you get it back at the latest when the procedure ends.
- **Knowledge test:** the canton's pages and handbook do not say how long a pass stays valid. If you passed some time ago, ask your commune whether the result is still accepted.

## A sensible order

1. Check that you are in the Swiss civil status register. If not, register now. It can take months.
2. Ask your commune whether you take the German and knowledge tests before or after filing, and book them.
3. Within 3 months before submitting, collect proof of your current activity. Within 6 months, order the civil status document.
4. File online at zh.ch/e-einbuergerung and upload everything.

For many people the knowledge test is the biggest thing to study. The free questions show you how you are doing.

## Page: The Zurich Knowledge Test: Format, Topics, Preparation

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/knowledge-test/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/grundkenntnistest/  
Last checked: 2026-10-30

## What the test is for

If you apply for ordinary naturalisation in the canton of Zurich, you must show that you know Switzerland, the canton and how Zurich communes work. The knowledge test (Grundkenntnistest) checks this. According to the canton's 2025 study, all Zurich communes now use the cantonal test.

## Who has to take it, and who does not

The canton lists these exemptions. You do **not** have to take the test if you:

- are under 12,
- are currently in compulsory school or in upper-secondary training in Switzerland (Gymnasium, apprenticeship),
- have completed five years of compulsory school in Switzerland, at least three of them at lower-secondary level,
- have an upper-secondary qualification from Switzerland.

Your commune decides whether an exemption applies to you. The canton offers a self-check.

## What does the test look like?

The canton's page gives **no number of questions, no duration and no pass mark**. It refers you to your commune.

A 2022 press report mentioned 50 questions in 60 minutes, with 30 correct answers to pass. The canton has not confirmed these figures; your commune can tell you the format and pass mark.

The canton publishes its question catalogue in German only, so expect the test in German.

## The topics

The canton's question catalogue has four areas, with questions on the Confederation, the canton and the commune:

1. **Democracy and federalism**
2. **Social state and civil society**
3. **History** (Confederation and canton)
4. **Geography** (Confederation and canton)

## How to prepare

On its page the canton provides, free of charge:

- a **practice test**,
- the **brochure on naturalisation and the knowledge test** (PDF, 76 pages, German; printed copies from your commune),
- the [list of all questions](https://www.zh.ch/content/dam/zhweb/bilder-dokumente/themen/migration-integration/einbuergerung/gkt/grundkenntnistest_kanton_zuerich.pdf) (PDF, 78 pages, German).

The Federal Chancellery's [The Confederation in brief](https://www.bk.admin.ch/bund-kurz-erklaert) is an easy introduction to the political system. The canton also suggests a few books as optional reading.

We do not reproduce any question from the catalogue here. Read it on the canton's page.

## Registration and cost

You register through your **commune**. It tells you where and when. Depending on the commune, you can take the test before or after you file the application. The cost depends on the commune and the provider. The canton gives no figure. Ask your commune.

Questions about the test go to the Gemeindeamt, naturalisation section: grundkenntnistest@ji.zh.ch, telephone +41 43 259 83 81.

## How our practice fits in

Our practice questions are **original questions that we wrote**. They cover the same topics as the test but are not the canton's questions. You study first in your own language, then in German, the language of the test.

## Next step

Try the [free questions]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/free-practice/).

## Page: Language Certificates for Naturalisation: What Counts

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/language-certificates/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/sprachzertifikate/  
Last checked: 2026-10-30

## Levels required

For ordinary naturalisation the Confederation requires a national language at **level B1 spoken and A2 written** (Common European Framework of Reference, CEFR). B1 means you can express yourself clearly in familiar situations and follow the main points of clear conversation. A2 means you can read and write short, simple texts.

Cantons may ask for higher levels. In the canton of Zurich, the page on ordinary naturalisation gives B1 spoken and A2 written. Check the rules of your own canton.

## Which proofs count

According to the SEM, one of these is enough:

- the language is your **mother tongue**,
- you completed **five years of compulsory school** in that language,
- you completed **upper-secondary or tertiary education** in that language,
- you hold a **certificate on the SEM list**.

Course attendance confirmations and online self-tests are not enough. If you have a serious disability, illness or learning difficulty, you can submit a medical confirmation. The authority then decides how to proceed.

## The SEM list

The SEM keeps a list of recognised language certificates and updates it continuously. When we checked, the list was dated 1 October 2026. It applies to naturalisation and to procedures under foreign-nationals law. The list includes, among others, certificates from Goethe, telc and ÖSD, and the **fide language passport**. The canton of Zurich also names telc, Goethe, ÖSD and fide on its page. Check the current list for the level and the exam parts that your certificate covers.

The canton of Zurich also offers the **Cantonal German Test**. It has an oral part and a written part with listening, reading and writing. The canton's page has a model test to practise with.

## The fide language passport

fide is a system developed on behalf of the Confederation. The fide test checks German at levels A1 to B1 with everyday situations in Switzerland.

- The test has an **oral part** (speaking and understanding, 40 minutes) and a **written part** (reading and writing, 60 minutes). You can take both parts together or separately.
- There is no pass or fail. The **language passport** shows one level for oral and one for written.
- You receive the passport by post about four weeks after the test.
- The written part requires Swiss standard German, not dialect.
- If you already have B1 or better, you can use the **fide dossier** from age 16: you submit documents and have a meeting. The passport then records B1.

fide does not say how long a language passport stays valid. Ask your commune whether an older one is accepted.

## Where and how to take the exam

You take the fide test at an accredited exam institution. fide lists them by canton and city, with exam dates. Register at least 15 days before the date. A preparation course is not compulsory. fide's page has a free model test to practise.

## Typical prices

The whole fide test costs **CHF 250**, the oral part alone CHF 170, the written part alone CHF 120. For other certificates and for the Cantonal German Test in Zurich, the pages give no fixed price. It depends on the provider and the commune.

## Exemptions in the canton of Zurich

You do not need the Cantonal German Test if German is your mother tongue, if you are under 12, if you completed five years of compulsory school in German, or if you hold an upper-secondary or tertiary qualification taught in German. You are also exempt if you already have a certificate showing B1 spoken and A2 written. The full list is on the canton's page.

## Next step

If you are preparing for the knowledge test in Zurich, the [free questions]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/free-practice/) also help you practise your German.

## Page: What Naturalisation Costs in the Canton of Zurich

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/fees/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/gebuehren/  
Last checked: 2026-10-30

## Three levels, three fees

For ordinary naturalisation in the canton of Zurich you pay the Confederation, the canton and your commune. Then there are the costs of the language proof and the knowledge test. The canton says the fees of the canton and the Confederation are fixed. Each commune sets its own fee.

## Overview (in CHF)

| Who | Confederation (SEM) | Canton of Zurich | Commune |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Adults aged 25 and over | 100 | 500 | set by the commune |
| Couple, joint application | 150 | 500 | set by the commune |
| Under 25 | 100 (under 18: 50) | 250 | half the communal fee |
| Under 20 (applications from July 2023) | 100 (under 18: 50) | free | free |
| Children included in a parent's application | free | free | free |
| Application is rejected | 300 | 200 | the commune's fee |

Source: the canton of Zurich's fee table. The SEM gives the federal fee as CHF 100 per adult, CHF 150 per couple, and CHF 50 for minors who apply on their own.

## Communal fees

Communes set the fee themselves. A 2025 study by the canton shows, for people aged 25 and over: the fee is most often **between CHF 400 and 600**. Overall it ranges **from CHF 200 to CHF 2,400**. Your commune will tell you the exact amount. Not every commune publishes it online.

## Language test

The cost depends on the proof.

- **fide test:** whole test CHF 250, oral part only CHF 170, written part only CHF 120. These are the prices on fide's page.
- **Cantonal German Test and other certificates:** the canton says fees differ by commune and language school; there is no single price.

## Knowledge test

The canton gives no amount. The cost depends on the commune and the provider. Ask your commune.

## Are fees refunded?

Neither the Confederation nor the canton publishes a refund rule, and the canton's table charges fees even when an application is rejected. Assume that fees you have paid are not refunded.

## Other procedures

Simplified naturalisation of a spouse living in Switzerland costs CHF 900 at federal level. It is paid in advance and is not refunded. See the SEM for details.

## Next step

Fees are only part of the cost. With the [free questions]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/free-practice/) you can see how ready you are for the knowledge test before you spend money on it.

## Page: Residence Years Calculator

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/calculator/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/rechner/  
Last checked: 2026-10-30

## What the calculator does

For ordinary naturalisation you need ten years of residence in Switzerland. The calculator helps you make a rough count. You enter your date of birth and your periods of residence. It shows the total and how many years are still missing.

## The rules it applies

- **Years between your 8th and 18th birthdays count double.** If you lived in Switzerland from age 8 to 18, that gives ten years.
- **At least six years must be actual years in Switzerland.** Doubling alone is not enough.
- **Three of the last five years before the application** must be spent in Switzerland.
- **The type of permit matters:** B, C and Ci count in full, F counts by half, N and L do not count.

Cantons and communes also set their own residence periods. The calculator does not check them.

## What it does not do

The calculator counts years. It does not decide whether you can be naturalised or which years count: that is up to the authority handling your application. The canton also has its own self-check.

## Next step

If your years add up, preparing for the knowledge test is the next job. Try the [free questions]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/free-practice/).

## Page: Free Practice for the Zurich Knowledge Test

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/free-practice/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/kostenlos/  
Last checked: 2026-10-30

## What you get for free

- **30 sample questions** for the canton of Zurich, with no account. Each question has a short explanation. You see it in German and in your own language.
- **One free mock test** after you sign up with your email address. Like the real test, it is in German and has a time limit.
- All pages of this guide.

## Where the questions come from

We write all questions, explanations and translations ourselves. They cover the same topics as the canton's test but are not the canton's questions. Each answer is based on pages of the Confederation, the canton or the communes.

## How to practise

First you learn the question in your own language, beside the German text. Later you practise in German only, as in the test.

## What the Viapunt Pass adds

The **Viapunt Pass for the canton of Zurich** costs **CHF 29** (one payment, 6 months of access) and includes:

- all questions, about 350, with explanations,
- all study modes: Learn, Practise and Mock test,
- unlimited timed mock tests in German,
- the "Explain this" button in your language,
- every language.

If you need more time, you can extend access by three months for CHF 9. Pay by card or TWINT.

## Next step

Start with the free questions. If they help, you can buy the Viapunt Pass.

## Page: Frequently asked questions

English: {{GUIDE_URL}}/en/faq/  
German: {{GUIDE_URL}}/de/faq/

### How long does naturalisation take?

The canton of Zurich says the procedure takes about two years. Processing in the communes has recently become slower on average. You can find the steps on the page [Zurich, step by step]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/zurich-step-by-step/).

### Are my children naturalised with me?

Minor children can be included in a parent's application. In the canton of Zurich they then pay no canton or commune fee, and none at federal level either. Ask your commune whether your child can be included. Costs are on the page [Fees]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/fees/).

### What happens if I fail the knowledge test?

The canton of Zurich's pages do not say. Ask your commune whether and when you can retake the test and what it costs. How to prepare is on the page [Knowledge test]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/knowledge-test/).

### Is the knowledge test in German only?

The canton of Zurich publishes its question catalogue in German only, so expect the test in German. More on the page [Knowledge test]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/knowledge-test/).

### Is this website official?

No. This service is independent and not connected to any authority. All practice questions are original and are not the canton's questions. The [overview]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/overview/) is a good place to start.

### Do translations help in the real test?

Translations help you learn, because you understand the content in your own language. The real test is in German, though. So later you practise in German only. Try the [free questions]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/free-practice/).

### How are residence years counted?

You need ten years in Switzerland, three of them in the last five years before you apply. Years between your 8th and 18th birthdays count double, but you must still have at least six actual years. The [calculator]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/calculator/) gives you a rough count.

### What does B1 mean?

B1 is a level of the Common European Framework of Reference for languages. You can express yourself clearly in familiar situations and follow the main points of clear conversation. Naturalisation needs B1 spoken and A2 written, see [Language certificates]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/language-certificates/).

### Do I need a C permit?

For ordinary naturalisation, yes: the Confederation requires a settlement permit C. Simplified naturalisation has different rules, for example for spouses of Swiss citizens. More in the [overview]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/overview/).

### Where can I find my commune's requirements?

On the website of your commune of residence, usually under "Einbürgerung" (naturalisation). There you find the checklist, the fee and dates. In the canton of Zurich the Gemeindeamt also helps, telephone +41 43 259 83 81. See also [Zurich, step by step]({{GUIDE_URL}}/en/zurich-step-by-step/).
